strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practical problem setting: channel-wise asynchronous sampling with fixed but distinct periods, combined with block-wise test-time missingness. This is a well-motivated gap between standard forecasting benchmarks and real deployments, and the paper clearly articulates why interpolation/downsampling preprocessing is problematic (Appendix B provides a useful spectral-distortion analysis).

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer is a coherent design: frequency-adaptive dynamic patching, channel tokens acting as read-only global anchors, and unified masked attention that handles variable-length inputs and missing patches within a standard Transformer. The masking scheme (Figure 3) is simple and cleanly implemented without architectural modification.

The experimental evaluation is thorough: four datasets including a real industrial LNG carrier dataset, two evaluation scenarios, a comprehensive set of strong recent baselines across architectures (TimeXer, iTransformer, PatchTST, TimeMixer, TimesNet, CrossGNN, DLinear), full results with error bars over 5 seeds (Tables 13-14), ablations for each of the three claimed challenges (Dependency/Asynchrony/Missingness), masking-strategy ablations, channel-token granularity analysis, input-length robustness tests, and a frequency-domain fidelity analysis. The model is also shown to be competitive in the conventional regularly-sampled setting (Table 11), addressing generality concerns.

Fairness concerns are partially anticipated: baselines are additionally evaluated under forward-fill inputs (Table 12), all models are evaluated on the same observed ground-truth targets, and the CMSE/CMAE metrics are well defined for heterogeneous horizons.
The paper is well written, with clear problem formulation, and the appendices provide sufficient implementation detail for reproducibility (hyperparameters, dataset configurations, hardware).
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental. The core ingredients are existing techniques: patch masking/dropout (PatchTST, PatchDropout), read-only attention (from vision-language prompt attention), channel/variate tokens (similar to memory or register tokens, and exogenous variate tokens in TimeXer), and frequency-based patching. The contribution is a careful combination and adaptation of these to the asynchronous/missing setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The 'practical' benchmarks are synthetically constructed by downsampling existing datasets (ETTm1, Weather, Monash) to artificial channel-specific rates. The asynchrony pattern is thus manufactured rather than observed, which weakens the central claim that results demonstrate robustness under real-world conditions; only the CHS dataset is genuinely real, and it uses a curated subset of 10 of 52 channels.

Missing direct comparison with irregularly-sampled time series methods (e.g., mTAN, RAINDROP, ContiFormer, or recent irregularly-sampled forecasting models listed in Related Work). The authors argue the setting differs (fixed per-channel periods), but these methods could plausibly be adapted and benchmarked, and their absence leaves the positioning incomplete.

There is an inherent evaluation asymmetry: baselines are forced to consume interpolated inputs while CTF consumes native non-interpolated data. Although the forward-fill variant (Table 12) partially mitigates this, a stronger design would be a shared representation where all models access the same observed points (e.g., mask-aware inputs for baselines).

Improvement margins over the strongest baselines are modest on some datasets (e.g., ETT1 CMSE 0.398 vs. PatchTST 0.414), and the model does not clearly separate from PatchTST (channel-independent) in all cases, leaving the benefit of explicit cross-channel modeling somewhat ambiguous in the asynchronous setting.

Scalability of unified attention is quadratic in the total token count and acknowledged by the authors as a limitation; no efficiency/compute comparison against baselines is reported despite the channel-wise token expansion.

The forecast horizon must be fully observed by assumption, and the number of channel tokens and masking ratios require dataset-specific tuning, which adds deployment complexity that is not fully discussed.

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant and underexplored problem setting: channel-wise asynchronous sampling and block-wise test-time missingness in multivariate forecasting, with a clear articulation of why conventional alignment/interpolation pipelines are problematic (Appendix B offers a useful spectral distortion analysis).

The proposed architecture is coherent: channel tokens as read-only aggregation anchors, unified masked attention, and frequency-adaptive patching are sensibly combined, and the masking taxonomy in Appendix C.2 is a thoughtful design-space exploration.

Evaluation coverage is broad in quantity: four datasets (including one real industrial LNG dataset), two scenarios, multiple missing ratios, ablations of all three claimed components, 5-seed error bars, conventional-setting results (Table 11), and masking-strategy ablations.
Writing and figures are generally clear, and the paper is honest about limitations (scalability of full attention, MSE-induced amplitude attenuation) in the Discussion.
weaknesses: Benchmark construction is arguably circular and favors the proposed method. The 'practical' datasets are created by the authors via channel-specific downsampling, and the test-time missing blocks are injected so that each block 'spans exactly one patch length' (Appendix A.2). Since CTF's core mechanism is patch-level masking, this design directly aligns the synthetic corruption with the model's inductive bias, and even allows the training mask ratio (t=0.4) to be tuned against the test corruption process (Table 15). This weakens the central empirical claim of 'robustness to real-world missingness.'

Missing baselines from the most relevant literature. Despite an extensive related-work section on irregularly sampled time series (ContiFormer, mTAN, Raindrop, IP-Net, transformable patching GNNs, etc.), none of these models are compared. The argument that 'each channel is regularly sampled but at different periods' does not justify their exclusion—they are the natural competitors for partial observability, and a fair comparison would clarify whether a specialized architecture is needed at all versus a well-tuned irregular-time-series model.

The headline quantitative gains are small and potentially confounded. In Table 1, CTF beats TimeXer by ~0.02 CMSE; the spectral analysis (Table 6) shows differences of 0.001–0.002 across bands, which is far too marginal to support the claim that interpolation distortion 'translates to improved trend and periodicity retention.' Moreover, baselines are trained on linearly interpolated data while CTF sees native-resolution inputs, so the comparison conflates preprocessing with architecture even though the appendix attempts to control for it.

Scalability of the method is a serious unresolved limitation. The unified attention concatenates all local tokens across all channels, giving quadratic cost in the number of channels/tokens. All experiments use at most ~21 channels (10 for CHS); the paper concedes this limits high-dimensional forecasting, which is precisely where inter-channel dependency modeling matters most in practice.

Incremental novelty. Channel tokens are a straightforward extension of read-only prompt tokens [21] plus channel embeddings; patch dropout during training is adopted from [28, 34]; frequency-based patch length selection is a known idea. The main new element is the masking matrix, and Table 10 shows that alternative maskings (CD-ReadOnly-Indexed) perform identically, suggesting the specific design contributes little.

The real-world evidence is thin: the CHS dataset contributes 10 hand-picked channels out of 52, is not publicly available (reproducibility concern), and is used only in Scenario 1. Combined with three author-modified benchmarks, the entire empirical story rests on data configurations controlled by the authors.

Several analyses are under-powered or single-dataset: the input-length robustness test (Table 5), channel-token count (Table 4), and masking-strategy comparison (Table 10) are each confined to SolarWind, limiting generality of the conclusions.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: the combination of channel-wise asynchronous sampling, cross-channel dependencies, and block-wise test-time missingness in multivariate forecasting. The problem formulation (Section 3) and the proposed CMSE/CMAE metrics are clearly defined and likely useful to future work.

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer is a coherent design: frequency-adaptive patching, channel tokens as read-only attention anchors, and masking-aware unified attention each map onto one of the three identified challenges, and the architecture is implemented without modifying the standard Transformer.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: two scenarios (asynchrony; asynchrony + block-wise missingness at multiple ratios), four datasets including a genuinely new real-world industrial dataset (LNG CHS), seven strong baselines, full results with 5-seed error bars in Appendix E, plus an additional conventional-setting benchmark (Appendix D) demonstrating the model is not worse in the standard setting.

Ablations are comprehensive and well-designed: component-wise removal (Table 3/9), masking-strategy comparison (C.2), number of channel tokens, train-time masking ratio (Table 15), and input-length robustness (Table 5). The frequency-domain analysis (Section 6.3, Appendix B) is a nice touch that connects interpolation-induced spectral distortion to forecasting quality.
The paper is honest about limitations (scalability of full attention with channel count, MSE-induced amplitude attenuation) in the conclusion and Discussion.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: channel tokens are essentially per-channel CLS tokens, and the individual ingredients (patch dropout [28], read-only masking [21], FFT-based patching) are existing techniques recombined. The paper's strongest claim is the problem setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, so the contribution rests heavily on the benchmark construction and empirical evidence.

Baseline fairness and coverage concerns: (i) the compared models were all designed for regular, fully observed inputs and are given zero-filled missing blocks, which is arguably an adversarial choice—stronger baselines combining baselines with imputation (e.g., forward-fill, learned imputation, or irregularly-sampled TS models such as mTAN, T-PATCHGNN, ContiFormer, Imts-mixer, several of which are cited but not compared) are missing despite being natively capable of variable-length inputs; (ii) this makes the magnitude of the claimed superiority hard to calibrate.

The 'practical' benchmarks are synthetically constructed by heuristically downsampling existing benchmarks (ETT1, Weather, SolarWind); the sampling periods are assigned by the authors rather than observed. Only the CHS dataset (10 selected channels) is truly real-world, which weakens the central claim that the proposed setting 'reflects real-world conditions'.

Scalability is a significant unaddressed concern: attention is quadratic over all local + channel tokens across channels, yet no experiment exceeds ~21 channels. High-dimensional sensor datasets (100+ channels) are exactly where the claimed real-world relevance would matter most.

Some improvements are modest and the analysis in Section 6.3 is close to noise (dominant frequency difference 0.0098 vs 0.0099; band-wise RMSE differences of ~0.002), which overstates the spectral-fidelity advantage.

Key design details are under-specified: the fallback patch length when no dominant frequency is detected ('based on the channel's relative sampling period') is vague; how the FFT-dominant frequency is made robust on non-stationary channels is not discussed. No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the bespoke dataset modifications.

The CMSE metric averages per-channel MSE over differing horizon lengths; its sensitivity to channel subsampling of the test set (noted in Appendix A.2) deserves more scrutiny as the sole evaluation criterion.
